utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everybody. Good morning, Ambassador Okun.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Karadzic. We're here to continue the cross-examination. I was advised we are having a new member from Mr. Harvey's team. Could you introduce --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] my colleague -- I'm sorry. I'm assisted now by my microphone and by Ms. Colleen Rohan, with your consent. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Welcome, Ms. Rohan. Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Ambassador.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Have you had a good rest? Did I tire you out on Friday?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I hope so. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I should like to go back to one point. You said that you were concerned because in the 1981 census there weren't many Yugoslavs and that that was a sign that Yugoslavia does not have a lofty future?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, Dr. Karadzic, it was not I who said I was concerned, but I said that the highest of our intelligence authorities, the National Intelligence Council, in a report, they called them estimates, NIE, National Intelligence Estimates, they had said that the fact that the small -- relatively small number of people had identified themselves as Yugoslavs indicated that the state was ripe for some kind of nationalist trouble. It was not my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, that is right. Now, I should like to ask you this: Well, it's another reason why I envy Mr. Tieger for having been able to meet with you, and then receive very brief answers when he examined you. So could you treat me in the same way as well, please. Thank you. Do you agree that in 1981, most of the Yugo enthusiasts were among the Serbs, and the least among the secessionalist Slovenes, Croats, and Muslims, secessionist oriented?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know the answer to that. I was in Berlin, Germany, in 1981, for the next several years, and was not following Yugoslav affairs, but I can understand that that might have been the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, that was a shorter answer than the first one. Now what I want to ask you is this: Was that, in a way, in civilian life, the political spectrum, a type of desertion from Yugoslavia, just as in 1991, people deserted from the Yugoslav People's Army, having been on its list? Do you know that the Slovenes, Croats, and Muslims left the Yugoslav People's Army far before the outbreak of the war?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was made aware of that when I was in Yugoslavia. In answer to your earlier question, did that represent a desertion from Yugoslavia, again, I cannot answer. One could answer that by looking at the previous censuses. If 1961 and 1971 showed many, many more people declaring themselves Yugoslavs, well, then 1981 would make a difference. But I'm not aware of the censuses of 1951, 1961, 1971, so I just don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But can we agree that in the Yugoslav People's Army, it was -- just as in Yugoslavia, it was mostly the Serbs that remained, the majority who remained were Serbs?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And would you also agree that at the first democratic elections, seven members of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina were elected, two Serbs, two Croats, and two Muslims, and one representative of the minorities or, rather, those who weren't Serbs or Croats or Muslims?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that the Serbian Democratic Party, for that position, nominated the leader of the local Jewish community, Mr. Ceresnes, who was not a member of our party?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well, but it's a fact. Now, do you know that the Muslims -- or, rather, the SDA put forward, as a nominee to that position that went to the minorities, Ejub Ganic, who was from Sandzak and, in our opinion, a Muslim extremist?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of that. I'm also aware that he declared himself a Muslim after he was elected on the Yugoslav list.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, can you understand that we considered that this was trickery and that we were angry and upset, insulted?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, when you came to Yugoslavia in a position of the NATO command as a political adviser after the major crisis that took place in 1971 and the replacement of the Croatian leadership, and then in 1972 the replacement of the Serb leadership, in the West, did the West have an interest in the oppositional forces in Tito's Yugoslavia at that time? Were they interested in them, the forces of the opposition?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They, of course, followed the situation in Yugoslavia, those experts in it, people like Mihajlo Mihajlov were known even to the general public, but as a matter of policy, they supported Marsal Tito and the territorial integrity of Yugoslavia, because their principle concern was the Soviet Union.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: At the time, did you know anything about Alija Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that at that time, the Muslims, at the level of the federal state, occupied significant positions and wielded significant influence?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were well represented.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, do you remember that the ideological basis for Yugoslavia's unity was brotherhood and unity, which was proclaimed by Tito in order to enable the existence of both diversity and unity?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you agree that the Communist Party of Yugoslavia was the connecting tissue holding together the Yugoslav peoples and republics together?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Up to a point, but not completely. The Communist Party, after all, did not represent the broad masses of the country. It may have claimed to do so, but it did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But would you agree that given that situation, a party who does not have the support of the party [as interpreted] can only rule through a dictatorship?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't agree to that. To say that unless you rule as a Communist, you must rule as a dictator, is a proposition that I don't think I could support, and, in fact, I don't think it is defensible. Surely, there are many countries that do not have Communist dictatorships - who used to have them - who have perfectly democratic countries now. We see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But you will agree, I'm sure, that the crisis, for example, that ended in Croatia in 1971, was, first and foremost, a secessionist crisis, and that Croats at the time could have elected to step down -- had they been able to vote at the time, the Croats would have voted to step down from Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's possible. I'm not certain. I don't think anybody can be certain of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I'm wondering about the relevance of this line of questions. Could you move quickly to the relevant issues.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellency. I was just about to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, do you agree that it's very important who the political -- or what the political profile is of the main actors in the Bosnian-Herzegovinian crisis; for example, that that is of great importance, what their political history is and political intentions are?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's important.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: My thesis and case, Mr. Ambassador, is that Alija Izetbegovic, already in 1939, was among the founders of the Young Muslims, which the Muslim organisation in Bosnia-Herzegovina held as an affiliation of the Muslim Brothers from Egypt; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you're not denying it either; right?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm neither confirming it nor denying it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, my next question: Do you know that the great Jerusalem Mufti al-Husseini in 1943 on two occasions visited Bosnia-Herzegovina, and people say that he was an uncle of Yasser Arafat, which is of no great importance, but, anyway, that he was a great Hitler ally in the Middle East?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you know that he was a guest of honour of Alija Izetbegovic, and that his visits resulted in the creation of one and then another one SS Waffen and Handzar Division, composed of Bosnian Muslims?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know about the Handzar Division. "Handzar" means "scimitar," during World War II, 66 years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, do you know that that organisation, the Young Muslims, led by Alija Izetbegovic and his group, continued secretly to act within Yugoslavia even after World War II?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that. I suspect it's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And because of that, the group was tried and given prison sentences in 1947, I think it was. But, anyway, I'd like us to move on to present-day times and ask you: Do you agree that Alija Izetbegovic, otherwise a very persistent man and with set views, continued that kind of activity even when he was released from prison. And in 1970, he was the author of the "Islamic Declaration," and other people just gave him advice?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I mentioned that yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that from 1970 to 1980, he disseminated the "Islamic Declaration" through Islamic circles, and in the 1980s, he started creating the nucleus of an organisation which was supposed to put into practice the "Islamic Declaration," and he was tried because of that at the Court in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we now have 1D34 called up, please, or 0034. The document on e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Ambassador, here we have the judgement from 1983 of the District Court in Sarajevo, in which there were five judges, Muslims -- no, I beg your pardon. Three were Muslim, and one was a Serb, and another one was a Croat. And that is a judgement for the accused in the trial against Alija Izetbegovic et al, for the crime of association to engage in criminal activity under Article 136, et cetera, et cetera; and the trial was held from the 18th of July to the 19th of August, 1983. And on the 20th of August, 1983, this trial chamber passed a judgement stating that the accused Alija Izetbegovic and Omer Behmen, and Hasan Cengic, the accused Hasan Cengic - well, the first two were definitely tried in 1947 as well, but other accused appear here - were found guilty, Alija Izetbegovic and Omer Behmen, because at the beginning of 1974, after several occasions in the previous years, taken up with -- I had hoped that the interpreters have this document in front of them so I can speak quickly -- taken up with the idea of Islamic renaissance, and discussed the need for the realisation of this ideology and ideal, and after Alija Izetbegovic wrote and published texts of that kind, along with suggestions from Omer Behmen, wrote the text of the "Islamic Declaration," so the "Islamic Declaration" is something that he authored, and the group existed, and they formed an association for the purposes of hostile activity. Now, were you aware of this judgement before you came in to testify here?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The Western intelligence services exchanging information with NATO, did they warn the authorities of this group as a possible force which could play a significant role should there be development of events involving the Soviet Union?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea. I was not involved with Yugoslavia at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. May we now move on to the next page of that same document, or, rather, page 7. On e-court, yes, one page on, please. It's page 7 of the text. Page 7, please, yes. Thank you. Now, in that -- in the middle there, it says Omer Behmen, the second paragraph marked in Serbian -- Omer Behmen added on to the text about the Muslims in Yugoslavia, and in early 1982 returned the text to Behmen, agreeing to postpone publication. In the text entitled "Muslims in Yugoslavia," they noted that the emergence of the Partisans in World War II endangered the spiritual survival of Muslims. And then towards the end, they said that they view the Islamic revolution in Iran as their own revolution and as a true revival. And then later on, towards the Iraq-Iranian conflict and the Iranian revolution, and the victory of the Islam and Iranian resolution carried out by the corrupt regimes in surrounding countries, would represent great encouragement to the Muslims of Yugoslavia, and thereby they would turn a new page in their history. Do you consider --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. What is your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you consider that that was, indeed, the reason for the Serbs' concern?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can imagine that an exaggerated concern from the Communist government would result from reading anything to do with a religious nature. As we all know, Communist regimes were officially atheistic, by law, and in fact, so any religious declaration was bound to agitate them. Whether it was significant or not is another matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now may we have the next page displayed, please. Next page, yes. Now, Alija Izetbegovic, Omer Behmen, and Ismet Kasumagic, that's the title. And then: "In the summer of 1982 in Sarajevo, Alija Izetbegovic and Omer Behmen agreed, with the help of Teufik Velagic, a member of the hostile emigre organisation in Vienna and a signatory to the new democratic alternative, to contact the Iranian ambassador in Vienna in order to make a copy of 'The Islamic Declaration' available to the Iranian authorities and seek support for the positions set out in it, as well as to establish contact with the representatives of Iran's religious and political authorities with a view to seeking assistance and support for implementing the positions set out," et cetera. So is this not politics, too, in addition to being religion?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's politics. Of course, it represented, as you know, Dr. Karadzic, and I know, a wing of the SDA party that was by no means the majority wing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Ambassador. This was in the 1980s. In the 1990s, the same group formed the party, and we'll come to that in due course. Now, on page 12 of the Serbian text - may we have that displayed? - it says that from the beginning of 1979 to 1980 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you wait until the Ambassador can follow in English. If Mr. Karadzic is not following the Serbian version in the e-court, how about using only English so that the ambassador can see them easily and expand. Could you help find --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Yes, I'll try and identify it in the English version. It says here as follows, number 5: "From the beginning of 1979 until 1983," et cetera, "Alija Izetbegovic asserted that Islam must be a state system or social system in all Muslim countries, in all countries where the population is Muslim, and that the necessary conditions should be created to turn Bosnia and Herzegovina into an Islamic republic with Islamic laws in the future."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, my question to you, Ambassador, is the following: You met Mr. Izetbegovic several times, according to your note-books. During those meetings, did he disclose to you his intentions, that is to say, that Bosnia should become an Islamic republic with Islamic laws --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did not say that, nor did the other Muslim leaders who we dealt with frequently; Haris Silajdzic, for example, and others, who were completely secularised in their behaviour. Ejub Ganic, as we already mentioned, turned out to be a Muslim, after running and being elected as a Yugoslav in the 1990 elections. He was thoroughly secular in his view. Zulfikarpasic, one of the founders of the party and one of the funders of the party, was a very wealthy businessman, and he was entirely secular in his view. And Fikret Abdic, the SDA candidate who received the most votes in the 1990 presidential election, was also entirely secular in his view. So you are going into a lot of detail which is, of course, interesting from the historical point of view, but does not represent the state of affairs in the SDA.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You will see that it does, actually. Did you trust them when they portrayed themselves as secularised and secular? I'm talking about Izetbegovic and his group. I'm not talking about Zulfikarpasic and Silajdzic. Do you know they were frank and honest with you?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Izetbegovic never had -- never hid his religiosity, nor did our president, George W. Bush, who was often accused of this kind of stuff because he was a self-described born-again Christian. These are not unusual events in countries.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ambassador. Number 3 now in Chapter 5 says -- I think that you need to move on to the next page in English. It's probably the next page. Number 3: "In the summer of 1982 in Pazaric," at somebody's summer home, "he said that our imams should be armed and that they should interpret and apply Islam following the example of Iran's Shiite imams." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have page 16, Chapter 7; pages 13 and 14 in e-court, that is, in the English version. It's this document. And now on page 14 -- now on page 14, because Chapter 7 only begins on page 13 -- could I please have page 14 now? It's the next page. A bit further down, the bullet points, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The fifth bullet point or paragraph that: "An Islamic revival begins --" What is being referred to here is Hasan Cengic, one of the most important members of that group. You probably met him as well. It says here -- and he pointed out that an Islamic revival begins with a religious revival and is brought to a successful conclusion with a political revolution and the establishment of an Islamic government. The next paragraph: "That the goal of the Islamic revolution in our country is the creation of a unified Islamic state comprising the area of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Sandzak, and Kosovo." Do you agree that in that period of time from 1977 until 1981, Sandzak and Kosovo were in Serbia, and part of Sandzak is in Montenegro as well; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Next paragraph, please: "That Jihad should be pursued to its final outcome in order to exterminate the enemy and the infidels." And what is particularly highlighted is the following: "We should not wait for a challenge or a provocation. Muslims must invent a challenge. They must be the ones who produce the challenge, and the goal will then come by itself." Is that a cause for a concern among the non-Muslim population of Bosnia and Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it could be if these people had power or represented a majority inside their party, neither of which was the case. So I don't think it could be of much concern. Every country has its lunatic fringe of the right, or of the left, or of this or that religion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Ambassador. However, you would agree that if such people were to come to power, it would be very dangerous?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If they had full power and if they still believed this, it could be. But in the case of Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1990 and 1991, which is, after all, the subject matter of this discussion, the Muslims did not have an army, they had nothing, like any military force whatsoever. They were outnumbered by the Bosnian Croats and the Bosnian Serbs, both of whom were more highly organised and had their countries behind them. We've already discussed that in discussing the goals. So the chances of them ever putting this fanciful dream into action were nil. That, of course, is my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 16 now in e-court. Can we go on? Sorry, page 15 in English. Page 15 in English, Chapter 7. Could we please have the English version. I think that should be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We are continuing with the positions of Mr. Hasan Cengic as an important person within that group, that Muslims have to confront all non-Muslims and Communists. Paragraph 2: "They should be -- they, the Muslims should be prepared for self-sacrifice to achieve their goals." And then two paragraphs down, in the middle of the paragraph that starts with "The Koran iyet": "All believers -- do not take an infidel as your friend. Do not be friends with your fathers or your brothers if they favour the absence of our faith." He emphasised that marriages to non-Muslims should not take place because this leads to the assimilation and destruction of the Muslim nation. And then the next paragraph, that: "A Muslim woman should not nurse the children of a non-Muslim woman, and vice versa. A Muslim cannot receive the blood of or give blood to a non-believer. Muslims must be superior to all others, and every effort should be made to create an environment in which everyone will be of pure Muslim blood." Do you agree that this is hate speech, even speech based on racism?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is a form of millenialism. There are, of course, extreme views in every religion. This is not pleasant to read, but one would have to know what it represented in reality: Paper, as Stalin -- [Overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll get to reality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please do not interrupt the Ambassador's answer. Hear him out. Yes, the next question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm concerned about the time I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So Hasan Cengic is a religious person, but you think that this is not hate speech? He is involved in politics, after all --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he emphasised that marriages to non-Muslims should not take place. Many Christians, Jews, Hindus, believe that sort of thing. I don't believe it's hate speech.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What about this, Mr. Ambassador: Do not greet infidels, kill infidels, and infidels are those who are not Muslims. What would you term that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It surely is an extreme statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And what do you say to this: that an environment should be created that would be of pure Muslim blood?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I said, I think it's a millenarian kind of document that I wouldn't take seriously.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree, Mr. Ambassador. He is not speaking of the collapse of a Muslim world. He wants to see a collapse of all other worlds. He sees the victory of his Muslim world and the decline of all others. Don't you agree to that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he certainly is a Muslim nationalist. On the other hand, there are statements that are purely nonsensical in here. For example, if we look at the last paragraph of the document you have put forth, I quote: "That the economic situation in our country is a specific expression of God's wrath ..." Well, if you believe that, you're capable of believing anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretaiton] I'd now like to call up 1D94.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the previous document please be admitted into evidence, the judgement of the Court. Actually, it's not final yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: 34. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour, although, well, I mean, the weight is another story. But in terms of the admissibility, no, no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D73.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to remind the Trial Chamber that this is a judgement, a judgement of the trial chamber of the District Court in Sarajevo. 1D94 is the next document that I'd like to have, please. I would like to remind the Chamber that the president of that trial chamber was a Muslim, and that most of the judges were Muslim, and also most of the witnesses called were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, I'm grateful to you for your observation to the effect that this would not be that dangerous had this man not had power. However, this document from the 14th of December, 1993, shows what kind of power was given to that man. So this is the headquarters of the Supreme Command of the Armed Forces, and it says here in this order: "In war service in a unit of the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, according to a temporary war establishment, the following appointment is made: "In the Main Headquarters of the armed forces in the Sector for Logistics. "Cengic, father's name Halid, Hasan, at the establishment position of the deputy chief of the sector." Is the situation somewhat different now, Ambassador?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think it's any different at all. The date of the document is December 12, 1993. At that point, the SDA party, as a party, and, if you will, the Muslims inside the government, had hardly any armed forces. It is a well-known and established and indisputable fact, that 70 to 90 per cent of the front-line was occupied by Croatian forces, and as of this date, Bosnian Serb forces occupied 70 per cent of the country, so they gave this man some kind of propaganda position. There is nothing in this document that indicates he had a position of any power.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll get to that later. Let's just clarify one matter. You are right, up to a degree, that there was a significant secular line within the SDA. However, Ambassador, let me remind you that that line abandoned the SDA even before the elections in 1990. Zulfikarpasic, Filipovic, Lamija, and others, they left the SDA and they established the Muslim Bosniak organisation that ran in the election, and I think that they won between two to four MPs. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they left the party, and Zulfikarpasic set himself up comfortably in Switzerland. There were, however -- always, there was a very strong secular streak, a secular aspect, to the SDA. And as events have shown since the period we're discussing, the secular aspect has come forward, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You will see that that's not the case, actually. And may I remind you that Mr. Zulfikarpasic said that he left the SDA for the following reason: He claimed that the secret hardcore of the SDA, consisting of Young Muslims, is working in a conspiratorial manner behind the back of the party and the people, and that no one can oppose them. We'll deal with that tomorrow, since you've raised the subject.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now I would like to have document 1D34. Actually, 1D94, Excellency, can we have that admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will be Exhibit D74.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D34 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We are going back to that judgement. What page?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the Serbian version, it is 78 and 79, and then 140. Seventy-eight and 79 in the Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What is confirmed is that out of 63 witnesses called in the trial, 58 were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: English page. Is it 140?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to identify it now, Excellency. 65 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, in the lower part of the page we see that out of 63 witnesses called in this trial, 58 were Muslims. And then the next page deals with that as well. All the witnesses are listed, all witnesses who testified about the organisation of the Young Muslims that continued to operate in a different way. However, now there was this document, "The Islamic Declaration," as a basis for their activity. And now could I please have number 140 in Serbian, and now we're going to see which page it is in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What is your question about this to the ambassador?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you denying this, Mr. Ambassador, that out of 63 witnesses, 58 were Muslims?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I don't know it for a fact, but I'm certainly not denying it. I've never seen this document before.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Page 140, I'm going to read it in Serbian, that particular part. The judgement says, "In our situation --" soon you're going to see the text on your screen: "In our situation, consistently advocating this kind of ideology means going back to a fratricidal war, denying our independence and our non-aligned policy. There is no doubt that this kind of policy of nationalism --" actually: "... ethnic divisions and the establishment of an Islamic state in Bosnia, a political system based on Islam and the like could not happen in a socialist self-management Yugoslavia in an environment that is the so diverse, from an ethnic and religious point of view, that if any individual group were to prevail, that would be inconceivable, unless it were to be --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Have you to indicate the English page number so that the others could follow.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We'll attend to it. We have problems, too, Your Excellency, just like Mr. Tieger. Much, much later, much later, after this statement of the witness, it's at least 50 pages beyond that. The English page we have now -- I mean, in the Serbian version, it's 79 and we're moving on to 140, so it's at least 50 pages further on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If he has the ERN number -- or can you follow it? What's the ERN number of the B/C/S page? No. You found it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have it on our screens now. Now, let's just find it. Now, where's the beginning in our setting, in our situation? Is that not the right page? Here it is, yes, towards the middle. Yes. Yes, that's it, that's it. You see, so it's around the middle, "Pan-Islamic ideology": [In English] "... ideology in a domestic version, according to the authors of the declaration and their sympathisers, seeks to adapt itself to the changed circumstances and to modest conditions. Such an ideology, which has basically run its course in the region where once it could have had certain socio-political motives and real religious influence, has emerged again in circumstances of socialist self-management. "There is no doubt that such ideology, national and religious separation, the establishment of an Islamic state in Bosnia, a political system based on Islam, et cetera, could not come into being in a socialist self-managed Yugoslavia, in an environment which is ethnically and religiously so mixed that the predominance or total domination of one of the existing national groups is simply unimaginable, unless it were based on terror or even on foreign intervention and the use of coercion."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Ambassador, do you know that the Muslim side, throughout the conflict, coveted and openly asked for foreign intervention?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Since they [Realtime transcript read in error "you"] were losing, and you occupying most of the country and ethnically cleansing their population, they were desperate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ambassador, but we'll prove to you that that was not the case. The important thing is that from the very beginning, that is to say, from the beginning of 1992 - and do you agree with this? - that already in April, May, June, a requested foreign intervention?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. Before I answer that, could I call attention to the screen which has my previous answer incorrectly written?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It reads on the screen "since you were losing," and what I said was "since they were losing."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ambassador.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were quite -- as I said, since they were losing, they were desperate for foreign intervention, just as the Croatians hoped for foreign intervention in 1991. In neither case did they get it. But that the losing side wants help, I don't find that surprising.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, when do you pin-point the time when they begin losing?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They began losing much earlier than the opening of hostilities in March 1992. Because already in the fall of 1991, the JNA was distributing weapons to Serb paramilitaries, and in certain opstinas, particularly along the Bosnian side of the Drina River, the Serbs were organising themselves, as they had previously in Croatia, into SAOs, that is to say, Serb Autonomous Oblasts. This was reported at the time and known at the time. So the Bosnian Serbs, with the help of the JNA, were already preparing for something in the fall of 1991. That's not surprising, since war had already broken out in Croatia, but it does indicate some alertness on the part of the Bosnian Serbs and the JNA, and certainly no one would consider it a peaceful measure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Ambassador. You're giving me more work, but there's a certain amount of satisfaction in that, too. Now, when do you pin-point the beginning of the Muslim preparations -- the SDA preparations for war?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They hoped to avoid war because they were occupying the Presidency. As we've discussed, and I won't go into this, they had gained the support of the Bosnian Croats on the referendum of February 29-March 1, 1992, and they were joining the three other Yugoslav republics which had opted for independence. That they were actively preparing for hostilities, I didn't see any evidence of that. Indeed, as I've said, it was all on the other side, because when we first looked into this situation and became aware of it, they had hardly any men under arms at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if I tell you, Mr. Ambassador, that Mr. Izetbegovic, who, ex officio, as president of the Presidency, was the president of the Council for National Defence of the whole republic with all three communities in it, already in February 1991 formed a secret alliance for the defence of Muslims, if I put that to you, would you deny that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. It's either way, so I can't deny it, I can't confirm it. I hear you say it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And if I tell you that this alliance or council already in the following month, on the 31st of March, took the decision to form the Patriotic League, what would you say to that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And if I tell you further that the Patriotic League was formed already on the next month, that is to say, the 30th of April, what would you say to that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: What year are we talking about, Dr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: 1991, immediately after the elections. The elections were in November. The government formed in December -- or the Assembly in December; the government, December and January; February, the secret committee; March, the decision to set it up; and, April, the establishment of it. 1991 is the year.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And if I tell you, furthermore, Ambassador, that Halilovic, later the commander of the BH Army, Sefer Halilovic, I mean, and then afterwards Hasan Cengic too, already by the summer of 1991, in 103 municipalities, had their commands and units of the Patriotic League and Green Berets, what would you say to that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would say that they were responding to the creation of the SAOs, the Serb Autonomous Oblasts, which had begun in 1991, as I indicated, and they were surely responding to the fact that war in Croatia had already broken out, and the JNA, in spite of its protestations of neutrality, was clearly taking the side of the Serbs in Croatia. There was no question of that. So I suppose one could see this, from their point of view, as a small defensive measure, since, after all, they had no armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That's why I like your note-books much more than your subsequent thinking. But let me ask you something else: With that answer you have confirmed that it was legitimate to take countermeasures; somebody takes a measure and then it's legitimate to take a countermeasure; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that would depend on the nature of the countermeasure. I think that's all one could say about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, do you consider that political measures -- that you can take military countermeasures to the political measures that have been taken in a country, as was ours?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that would depend what the political measure was. If it were the case of a person or a coup occurring in a country, a coup d'etat, which would be most political and military, one might take countermeasures against that. We see examples of this every day, today on television; in Bangkok in Thailand, in Bishkek in Kyrgyzstan. It's a difficult question and depends very much on the individual situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You have now given an answer to the legitimacy of the JNA action in Slovenia and Croatia. But in Bosnia-Herzegovina, we're going to show and prove that the formation of the SAOs was a political response to the political measures taken by the Muslim government, the Muslim section of the government. And now you say that the formation of the Patriotic League, itself, so early on, in all mixed environments, was a legitimate response to the political proclamation of the SAOs, which did not have any function, they were just proclaimed as a protection from the violent secession of Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. I said the SAOs were protected earlier -- excuse me, were projected earlier, and I also said that given the history of the SAOs in Croatia, there was every reason to be suspicious of SAO activity, along with that of the JNA. That was my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Ambassador. Now, do you know when the decision was taken to establish the SAOs, and when did the SAOs actually start operating?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know when the decision was taken. I know that we first became aware that they were operating around October/November 1991. I'm speaking of the SAOs in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, thank you. Very well. Now, do you believe that of the 109 municipalities in Bosnia-Herzegovina, in 103 municipalities there were Serbs -- there were also Serbs, whereas in Western Herzegovina, in the Croatian municipalities, there were less Serbs and less Muslims?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Western Herzegovina and the Western Bosnia. Certainly, there are very few Serbs in Western Herzegovina. Western Bosnia, there were quite a lot of Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm only referring to a few municipalities. Of the 109 municipalities, 103 municipalities, in those, Sefer Halilovic, Hasan Cengic, Alija Izetbegovic, formed units which their neighbours, the Serbs, saw already at the end of the spring and beginning of the summer of 1991. Do you challenge that at all?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I can't answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But if that were true, would your stand hold water then, your position that the Serbs had no reason for concern?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if it were true that the one side had armed itself, that could be a reason for the opposing side to arm itself, except that we know, and this was unarguable, that in March of 1992, when hostilities began, the Muslims were unarmed, essentially unarmed, and the Serbs, both military and civilian, were well armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, this is a good pretext for us to clarify these matters. In fact, it's my task to throw light upon these events for the benefit of the Trial Chamber, but I would be happy if you were to come away with different conclusions rather than the ones that you came in with. And had we met just in the way that you met Mr. Tieger, we might have achieved that earlier on. But, anyway, I'd like to refer to your note-book again now, note-book number 1. The ERN number is 016-3378 to 016-3456, page 38.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, if you could mention the date, that would help me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, I'll give up on that. Never mind, let's move on. Let me ask you this: Did you always believe Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never always believed anybody.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we now have called up on e-court a Prosecution document, 65 ter 06534, and page 45 of that. It is note-book number 1, your note-book number 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's Exhibit 784. [Indiscernible] are in number 1, between 2nd and 13 September, Ambassador.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Here we have one of your entries: "Izetbegovic very disingenuous." As a comment in brackets.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes: "Comment: Very disingenuous," which indicated that I clearly disbelieved him on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May we now have note-book number 5, Prosecution number 65 ter 06538, next, please. And the page is 61.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Exhibit 788.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's on the right-hand side -- towards the bottom, it says: "I see no reason," Izetbegovic, "I see no reason for -- [In English] "I see no reason to sit down at the same table with the Serbs. Only another humiliation for us. Serbs captured the Jajce and Bosanski Brod after ceasefire was signed. Why believe them?" [Interpretation] And your comment was: [In English] "This is false. Jajce and Bosanski Brod fell in October. Cease-fire was signed November the 10th, 1992."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is that right?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. I haven't found the passage yet. Forgive me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It's on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we zoom down, then the Ambassador will be able to see a page of his own diary. May we pan down.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps it's helpful to note that it's a meeting of December 17th, 1992, commencing at what appears to be -- I've actually got that blocked out, but it looks around 12.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have it now. Excuse me, Dr. Karadzic. I'm very sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we scroll down, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What Izetbegovic was pointing to here was that by December 1992, in fact much earlier, the war was going so badly for the Bosnian Muslim side that they were very reluctant to sit down and talk with your side because of the war and because of the extensive ethnic cleansing that had already been carried out. In fact, it took a great deal of persuasiveness on the part of Mr. Vance and Lord Owen and myself to get them to come to Geneva in the first place. This is not unusual. Parties often don't wish to talk to each other. We saw that in the Greek-Macedonian dispute. We see it now in the Israeli-Palestinian dispute. So he was very reluctant to talk to your side because he was losing, and he couldn't expect to get much at the negotiating table. That's why he said, It would only be another humiliation for us. That's clearly what he was referring to. And he says: "Serbs captured Jajce and Bosanski Brod after the cease-fire was signed. Why believe them." And I note right after that, note B, note bene to myself, that the above is false; that Jajce and Bosanski Brod fell in October. So I think that shows we were aware of the situation and that we certainly didn't play partisan politics with the situation. We were dealing with Izetbegovic and yourself and your colleagues and the Croatians on a completely honest and open basis. And when one or the other side said something that wasn't true, if we were aware of it, we took it on board and we took it into account.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If it is convenient, we'll have a break now for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, the point I was making was that you had written down that Mr. Izetbegovic was saying something that was incorrect. I would like to draw your attention to the middle of the page where it says: "MA," and I don't know who you designated as MA: [In English] "Bosnian Serbs are ready. No, they must return territory. Let us not --" I can't read it right. "Let us not --"

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: "Argue."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "Argue," thank you. Sorry, who is MA?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: MA is Mate Atasari. He was our man who worked specifically on the treaty for Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, yes, he was the president of the Subcommittee for Bosnia-Herzegovina within the conference in the former Yugoslavia; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, within the Working Group.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The same document, diary 5, on page 62. Page 62, could we please have that on our screens? This is what you wrote down: [In English] "Izetbegovic says look at Sarajevo. Serbs break cease-fire." [Interpretation] The comment you wrote down, your comment, is: "Untrue, per UNPROFOR." Then -- actually, is this correct?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. What he said was not correct, and you notice the next entry says that Atasari angrily excoriated Izetbegovic's attitude.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry. Just to keep the record straight, Your Honour, I noted that the recitation from the diary is not complete and, therefore, not accurate. So if we're going to have the appearance that it's incorporated into the record in its entirety, I think the entirety of the excerpt from Mr. Izetbegovic's comments should be included, and then moving on to Mr. Atasari's comments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We have the diary now in evidence, and then if there's some supplementary comment needed, I believe Ambassador Okun can deal with it. And at the end of the cross-examination, you can deal with it during your redirect. So let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Excellency. That's precisely what I wanted to say, something along similar lines, but it certainly would not have been put as well. Diary number 7. 06540 is the Prosecution number, page 28. This is what you wrote --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Exhibit P790.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [In English] "Izetbegovic: Terrible shelling of Sarajevo last night, worst in three months. Member of Presidency report cannot believe military." [Interpretation] Wilson was called in: [In English] "According to our data, last night was a quiet night in Sarajevo, less firing and shelling than usual. Izetbegovic ignores this information and changes the subject." [Interpretation] Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What I'm trying to say to you is that that was our experience as well. Whenever we'd catch him out in something like that, he would just change the subject and he would not explain anything. Thank you. Now I would like to draw your attention to your testimony in the Krajisnik case on the 22nd of June, 2004. The page is 4360. This is what you stated then: [In English] "The Muslim goal was to have a state of B and H within its current borders, internationally recognised, for the state to be unitary, have a central government, and for a secular democratic state." [Interpretation] Do you remember having stated that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you believe that Mr. Izetbegovic gave up on his "Islamic Declaration" and everything that he had been convicted for six years before that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think a lot of water had passed under the bridge between the earlier period that you're referring to and this period of 1991, 1992, 1993. He was by no means the only person in the SDA. There were other people who counted. He was the president of the Presidency, as you, yourself, pointed out yesterday, not the president of the country. And perhaps most important of all, his side was losing a very serious war, and his capital city was being shelled on a daily basis by your troops, and so that the situation really had changed quite a lot.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I hope, Mr. Ambassador, that we won't have to call you back again, because in your answers you are making my work even more extensive. You're giving me more work. However, we see here that the international community realised even before the war that Bosnia -- that Izetbegovic wanted a different Bosnia outside Yugoslavia. And you say that the international community realised that, that it would be secular, unitary, but that it would be a democratic state; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bosnia-Herzegovina joined three other republics in declaring their independence from Yugoslavia. No argument about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm just asking whether what you stated was the way I quoted it. Do you remember -- you were following our crisis already and you were involved as a mediator on Mr. Vance's team. Do you remember that in the autumn of 1991, I asked Mr. Izetbegovic to say publicly that the "Islamic Declaration" was not his political and state programme? I asked him to renounce it, but he didn't do that. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Apart from the Serbs, did other non-Muslim politicians -- actually, I beg your pardon. Could you tell us, what was the stream within the SDA that was opposed -- successfully opposed to Izetbegovic's fundamentalist policy? What was that secular streak within the SDA?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've already mentioned that both Haris Silajdzic and Ejub Ganic, who were very influential in those days -- Silajdzic is now president of Bosnia, so he's maintained a position of importance - he was then foreign minister - that they were secularist, and there certainly were others. The military men that we met from the BiH Army, and there were not that many because we often didn't go to the front-lines, but they also, when we saw them at the negotiation -- at the negotiating table, were thoroughly secular in their outlook. So I think it's fair to say that there were different views within the SDA on the point of religion and state.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. May I remind you of the following: that these groups that were secular left the SDA, established their own parties, and became marginal; the MBO that was headed by the secularists, Zulfikarpasic and Filipovic, had only two or three members in Parliament. Silajdzic left the SDA and established his own political party for Bosnia-Herzegovina, likewise a minor party with a considerably smaller number of seats in Parliament than the SDA; whereas Fikret Abdic, during the war, proclaimed that Izetbegovic had turned all of Bosnia into a mass grave, and he left the party as well. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there's no question that Fikret Abdic was a political opponent of Alija Izetbegovic inside the SDA. I mentioned that -- we've mentioned that here. And he was, no doubt, more of a secularist, and Izetbegovic was more of a religious type, but that did not change the situation on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But it is a fact that all of them lost the elections in relation to the SDA; that always won more votes than they did, right?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the SDA was the established party, and particularly at this point did well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: But there were not many elections during the war, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: May I remind you of your diary number 4, Prosecution number 65 ter 06530, page 50. In e-court, it is page 24.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Exhibit P777.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Before that appears on our screens, Ambassador, may I ask you the following: Do you know what kind of relations we had with the MBO and Fikret Abdic? I mean the secular Muslims.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know that specifically. I would assume they were pretty good.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. We'll go back to that. That's what you assume. But when you got involved in our crisis as a mediator, we had reached a historic Serb-Muslim agreement with the MBO; that was July and August 1991, and we'll go back to that. And during the war, we signed a peace agreement with Abdic and supported each other. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a very complicated question, Dr. Karadzic, because by reaching an agreement with Abdic, you clearly were seeking to undermine the central government. The question then arises: Was Abdic committing treason against the government? I wouldn't say he was, but I wouldn't say he wasn't. What you were doing, and it's understandable, was seeking to exploit any division on the enemy side. And you also, as we know very well, co-operated with the Bosnian Croats while the fighting was going on. It was, after all, a three -way fight, not a two-way fight.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll go back to this page. You say in this diary: "Karadzic: Izetbegovic wants a Muslim republic." Did you report that to your team, to Mr. Vance's team, Mr. Vance and the others, that is?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we now please have Prosecution number 65 ter 06533, diary number 7, your meeting with Adzic and Milosevic, dated the 15th of April, 1992, one week into the war, that is. In the meantime, can you recall that the General Adzic was Chief of General Staff; right?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Chief of General Staff of the Yugoslav Army, yes.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Page 33 of this document, in the diary itself. Diary page 33, that is. E-court, 18, page 18. Adzic says: [In English] "Adzic: Izetbegovic wants absolute power in B and H." [Interpretation] Further on, Milosevic tells you the following on page 40 of this document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's look at the correct page.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 22 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What you wrote down, that Milosevic had said -- President Milosevic: [In English] "It's typical Islamic fundamentalism."

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was his view.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Did you report that to the UN, or perhaps to the USA; the Serb anxieties, that is?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was all reported to the UN Security Council and to the Secretary-General.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How about the United States?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We weren't working for the United States.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like to call up your diary number 1. The Prosecution 65 ter number is 06534. What you describe is your meeting with Mate Boban on the 9th of September, 1992. You do remember who Mate Boban was; right?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: He was the leader of the Croat people in Bosnia-Herzegovina at that point in time; right?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and during the entire period he was the leader of the Bosnian Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 38 of this document, this is what you wrote down. In e-court, it's the same page. This is what you wrote down: "Boban --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you wait until we have it. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [In English] "Boban: The war started when Izetbegovic rejected the Conference on Yugoslavia, principles for B and H. B and H cannot be a state for only one people. State of three communities. Even Communists recognised that." [Interpretation] Do you remember this meeting and this conversation?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I avoided describing our situation in religious terms, but you said that Serbs and Croats constitute a majority in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And if you look at the religious component of our conflict, can we say that Bosnia was a predominantly Christian country?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No party, none of the three ethnicities which were, for all intents and purposes, the same as the religions, had a majority. About 44 per cent of the country was Muslim, about 31, 32 per cent Serb, about 19, 20 per cent Croat. So if you add the Serb and the Croat together, you would get a slender majority.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ambassador. I was not speaking along ethnic lines, but I was speaking in terms of religion. If you have an "Islamic Declaration," or, rather, "The Islamic Declaration" as the foundation for a future system, is it possible, either democratically or by force, to materialise the objectives of the Muslim minority in relation to the Christian majority? I'm not talking along ethnic lines now. It is a fact that Serbs and Croats are both Christians; right? That is a fact. And it's also a fact that the Serbs and Croats were against a unitary centralised Bosnia-Herzegovina; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've already testified to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you then find it plausible that insisting on the SDA programme for a unitary Bosnia-Herzegovina is political violence, as it were?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I think that's a statement too far. The desire for a unitary state, as I've already testified, was a basic principle, a fundamental tenet of the goals of the Bosnian Muslims. They could not achieve that either on the battle-field or with the negotiators. The negotiators did not give them that, which is why the Vance-Owen Peace Plan called for a highly decentralised country, a democratic one. But there was no possibility that this goal of the Muslims could be achieved, short of a military victory, and it was never achieved, not in 1991, not in 2010.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You certainly remember this position of Boban's and his insistence that Bosnia be a tripartite state, because it was even recognised by the Communists; right?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: His position, yes, on that point, was virtually identical to yours, as we have already discussed several times. Neither the Bosnian Croats nor the Bosnian Serbs accepted the idea of any form of centralised state. Each one had its own -- excuse me. Each one had its own self-proclaimed unit. You had the Republika Srpska, and Mate had the Community of Herceg-Bosna, and both of you wished to divide the state into what was variously referred to as a federal state, a confederal state, a cantonised state. You'll recall you often used the term "composite state." That is three statelets within the boundaries of Bosnia, which would have effectively meant there was no central state.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, Mr. Ambassador, that we, the Serbs, gave up on remaining in Yugoslavia and accepted the external borders of Bosnia-Herzegovina on condition that inside it be transformed, and that we called Bosnia and Herzegovina "South Switzerland"?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember "South Switzerland," but I do remember a formal acceptance of the situation by your people. But in reality, you never accepted it. The Bosnian Serbs never accepted at any time the Government of Bosnia-Herzegovina. After all, that's what the war was about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, do you deny that my and our official position was not division, but transformation of Bosnia-Herzegovina? That was the position taken by us publicly and advocated by us during the negotiations with the international mediators and the other two parties in Bosnia; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not so. What you've just said, Dr. Karadzic, division was -- and transformation, you make a contrast there, you say it was not division, but transformation; that is a distinction without a difference, because what you called transformation was, in fact, division. So I can't agree with you on that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you consider that Belgium is a divided country or partitioned country?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you consider that Brussels is a partitioned city or a divided city?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. But, on the other hand, if I may, there is no, quote, "Flemish republic" like the Republika Srpska, and there's no, quote, "French republic," like the Community of Herceg-Bosna. Your goals and the goals of Mate Boban were much more drastic than the linguistic divisions of Belgium.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Ambassador, I agree with you, because Belgium is a monarchy, so you can't have republics within a monarchy. But what would those units be called or entities be called if Belgium were a republic?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we would probably call them a linguistic unit, which is, in fact, what they are. One is French-speaking, the other is Dutch-speaking. Otherwise, the laws of the country are country-wide. There is no division on 95 per cent of the issues in Belgium, except the linguistic one. Your goal and the goal of Mate Boban was to have your own self-ruled area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Something like Catalonia in Spain; right?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Catalonia is an autonomous region. Its language is used officially. They would like to see it used more broadly, but it's not. Again, I would say that both Mate and your views at the time, and your stated goals, actually, were much more extreme than what we see in Catalonia. I would say that the ETA Basques who want to leave Spain probably would be close to the Bosnian Serb and Bosnian Croat position, but that's an arguable point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, it would be an arguable point, but we don't have time to go into that. However, let me remind you we accepted to remain in Bosnia. The Basques did not accept remaining within Spain. We accepted it under the conditions imposed by the European Community, or, rather, supported by the European Community. But let me ask you this, Mr. Ambassador: The Flemish, would they agree to us -- that we give them the name of a republic to avoid the ethnic name and anything referring to Flemish, but to say "the Flemish linguistic unit" or something like that, or would they name themselves and give themselves a name?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that matters very much. But if I could come back to a point you made a moment ago, Dr. Karadzic. It's important that the Court know that in all of this period that Dr. Karadzic and I are discussing, that the Bosnian Serb side insisted on having a veto power over any residual central government that would exist in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Dr. Karadzic has not mentioned that when he says that they were willing to live in Bosnia-Herzegovina, but it's an important point because this would have meant that the central government existed only on paper. And you'll recall, Dr. Karadzic, that when we discussed the constitutional principles, in particular, around September/October/November of 1992, you asked to have the veto power of the Bosnian Serbs even apply to the constitutional principles. I'm sure you remember that. I hope you do. It was a strong position. Yes, you said, There can be a Bosnia-Herzegovina as long as we have a veto power over any step the government takes. Of course, we could not agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And did I exclude the same right or did I -- was I against the others having the same right, the Muslims and the Croats, or did I say that each of the three communities should have the power of veto, and instead of the power of veto, you allowed three-quarters or four-fifths of a community -- you said they must vote for one unit? Did I ask for the power of veto only for the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, of course not. You were delighted that the other communities have the power of veto, because that would further viscerate any power that a central government, presumably a Muslim government, would have. So you were delighted to have everybody veto everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, do you think -- first of all, you said yourself that the starting standpoints in negotiations are always extreme ones, so do you think it's not legitimate to demand that the power of veto or qualified majority you use to fight the over-rule of people in a community, legitimately or not?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not illegitimate. And under the constitutional principles that were developed at the International Conference on the former Yugoslavia, the sides were given the power of veto over life-or-death matters, issues that were of deepest concern to the communities, but that ordinary acts of the government were not veto-able. That's the fourth principle, and those are the exact words, "not veto-able," and that's what your side objected to. You'll recall you introduced eight principles of your own at one point during the conference, which was very useful to us because you stated forthrightly what Republika Srpska wanted, except it was an impossible situation because it would have de facto dissolved any kind of Bosnian state.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does that then mean that the United States of America do not exist, because states within the United States of America have their own police force, their own constitutions, and their own autonomy, to a certain extent, and a whole range of issues which they are able to determine sovereignly, excepting the legislation at the level of the federal state, but, except for the FBI and other federal executive organs, the executive organs and authorities lie in the states of the United States of America? Does that mean that the United States of America lose their quality of being a state?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course not. But, Dr. Karadzic, if you'll excuse me, you've mis-described the situation. The United States is a federal government, consisting of 50 states. We all know that. They all have certain powers devolved to them. And according to our Constitution, Article 10, any aspect that is not explicitly given to the federal government may be devolved to the states. Now, in the Vance-Owen Peace Plan, that principle was applied to the 10 provinces. They were given police power, they were given all of the items you've mentioned, because the Vance-Owen Peace Plan called for a decentralised -- highly decentralised state with many powers given to the provinces, of which you had three majority provinces, and that would have left you, the plan sought, in a good position, just what you've described. But as you know, you rejected the plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ambassador. Did we reject the plan because of the constitutional principles or because of the maps?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You rejected it in toto, but your major concern was the map, I would think, particularly the issue of the corridor, Belgrade to Banja Luka, and other geographic areas; Popovo Polje, the Ozren Mountains. You're, of course, more well aware than I am of your positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. But let me remind you that we accepted the constitutional principles before the maps had been completed, and then we went on further. Now, do you remember that in Athens, on the 1st or 2nd of May, conditionally accepted the Vance-Owen Plan on the assumption that the National Assembly accept it? So could you tell me that, and if you could give me yes-or-no answers, that would be useful. Do you remember that in Athens, I conditionally accepted that plan, as far as I was concerned, and on condition that the Assembly also gave a positive view?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You signed the plan under the heaviest pressure. It was done very reluctantly. Koljevic and Krajisnik were in tears, almost, when you signed. And everybody knew that when you took the plan to the Serb Assembly, it would be rejected.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ambassador. But isn't -- don't all countries foresee that all such plans be ratified in their parliaments and assemblies? And, once again, may I ask you to give me yes-or-no answers wherever possible. Is it customary for plans of that kind to be ratified by the parliaments of the countries in question?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but Republika Srpska was not a country.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
