utterances.text: And why would Bosnia be more of a country than Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because it was recognised internationally, because it was a member of the United Nations, because it had all the attributes of a country, and Republika Srpska had none.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, I think that this is debatable, and we don't have time to go into that discussion. But let me remind you that an attribute of a state is the territory, the people, and effective power. Did Bosnia have territory, a peoples, and effective power over the whole of its territory? No, it did not. Whereas the Republika Srpska did; right?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: By force of arms and conquest, Republika Srpska did exist as a reality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll come to that. Thank you, thank you. Now, you're the right person for me to quote this following example to. You will remember that our priority was to retain Yugoslavia. The next priority was for Bosnia to remain in Yugoslavia. And in third place, we had that the Serb parts of Bosnia should remain within Yugoslavia. The fourth step was that we accept stepping down from Yugoslavia on condition that we be given our constitutional unit, constituent unit. Now I'd like to ask you: Do you know, Mr. Ambassador, how West Virginia was formed? Or, rather, let me shorten that question. During the Civil War, Virginia, or the largest portion of Virginia, decided to join the Confederation. The western part of Virginia refused to do so and remained within the Union, and the great President Lincoln decided that they had every right to that. And when the war ended, West Virginia continued to exist as a state; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You made that point frequently during the negotiations, so I'm well aware of your contention.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, would it be simple in Northern Ireland, for example, to decide for Northern Ireland to be attached to the Republic of Ireland? Would these drastic changes in the status of a state unit or territory be a simple thing to implement, to put into practice? You can once again give me an answer taking into account Flanders and that part of Belgium, if they were to decide that the whole of that area be attached to Holland or the -- well, in part to be attached to France, would they have the right to do that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it were done peacefully, if all parties agreed to observe the results, one could imagine that happening. With respect to the north of Ireland, that is a very contentious issue, has been for 80 -- 90 years, actually, since the republic gained its independence. All of these issues are complicated, Dr. Karadzic. What is not complicated is that the use of force of arms and ethnic cleansing be utilised to create pure majorities within a certain area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, Ambassador Okun hasn't come here as an expert. I allow such lines of questioning to go because those topics might have been subject of the conversation at the time, but please come to our issues, facts at the time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellency. I was just guided by the fact that the Ambassador, during the examination-in-chief, answered many questions put to him of an expert nature by Mr. Tieger, and those answers worry me because they can't stand without being clarified. But I will take your advice and return to material matters. May I have 65 ter 06538 next, please, called up on e-court. It's note-book number 5, where you describe the meeting with President Tudjman, the president of Croatia - right, Tudjman - on the 28th of November, 1992. And when that comes up on our screens, I'd like us to go to page 5 of that document, where President Tudjman informs you of the following --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excuse me. Is that a question to me?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The question is: You say that President Tudjman said: [In English] "Muslims want a Jihad, getting billions from Arabs." [Interpretation] Did you take President Tudjman seriously?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I always took President Tudjman seriously. But like all leaders, he was given to exaggeration and sometimes to prevarication. It was also no secret that the Arab states were helping the Muslims in Bosnia-Herzegovina. One had only to look at Haris Silajdzic's travel schedule. I think he earned quite a many frequent flyer miles between Sarajevo and Abu Dhabi.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You can do anything, Mr. Ambassador.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: On this point, Dr. Karadzic, if you'll notice, directly before President Tudjman makes a point about a Jihad, both he and Gojko Susak - that's the "GS" - talked about the, quote, "Posavina agreement," and he called that a fabrication by the Serbs, it never happened. Now, you had told us about an exchange - I'm sure you'll recall - of Kupres for the Posavina; Kupres to the Croats, the Posavina corridor to the Serb side. He said it never happened. You said it did happen. I cite this as an example of different parties telling different stories to the negotiators. That's part of our job, to sift out the various claims and decide which one is true or which one is not. Now, perhaps you'd care to tell us whether Kupres and Posavina agreement really happened. But I cite that in a -- not in a jocular vein, but to point out that in a negotiation that all the sides will say things that they believe support their position. That's not unusual.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You are a born and incorrigible diplomat, but unfortunately we can't turn this trial into our negotiations, the kind that we conducted, although I'd be happy to do that. Now, do you know, Mr. Ambassador, that I am the accused -- that I am accused of intending to expel a group, an ethnic group, and that you, on time, received information according to which Alija Izetbegovic and his group wanted to expel us not only from the federation but from the whole of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Did you receive and did the other American officials receive -- or mediators, UN mediators and American mediators, receive information telling them that the Muslim plan was to expel the Serbs from the whole of Bosnia-Herzegovina; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were aware that in certain areas, which were very small, Serbs were maltreated more by Croats than by Muslims, but that this went on. We were also aware of the overwhelming nature and the overwhelming difference between the Bosnian Serb actions and the Bosnian Muslim actions. And we have already introduced -- that is to say, the Prosecution has introduced statements by the president of the International Committee of the Red Cross, Dr. Sommaruga, and his chief delegate in Bosnia-Herzegovina, Thierry Germond --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: May I ask you, Mr. Ambassador --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- so we were aware of the actions people took on the ground. The policies that they had held or the views that they had held a decade earlier were taken into consideration, but as we say with the English proverb, actions speak louder than words, and we were interested in action.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would be very ready to debate this with you, but I see you have already taken the Prosecution's position, and I'm concerned about that, and that in your opinion this trial is superfluous. Now, let's go back to my question. You received information telling you that the Bosnian plan was to expel the Serbs from the whole of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that is to be found in note-book number 6, Prosecution 65 ter 0639, page 53, when you describe the meeting of the 12th of January, 1993 - 06539 is the number - with a delegation of the Bosnian Croats. Now, do you remember Mile Akmadzic, whom you mentioned? Was it during the examination-in-chief or my cross-examination? I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before that, Mr. Ambassador: You were said to have taken the position of the Prosecution. Do you have any comment on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes, I do have a comment. The position I expressed was mine. I know time is short, so we don't have time to go into it more deeply. I could certainly expand on what I said to you, but I've told you what I believe. And you are asserting that the Bosnian government held a formal position to expel all Serbs from Bosnia. I do not believe that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, let us see how you wrote down the words of Mile Akmadzic. I would like to remind you that this is the time when the negotiations were held concerning the Vance-Owen Plan, and Akmadzic is expressing concern as well as doubt as to the possibility of a peace agreement being reached. Have we found this page, Akmadzic, on the left?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This is Exhibit P789.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [In English] "Akmadzic against all four Muslim radicals wants to rid BH of Serbs. "Ganic, Silajdzic, Halilovic and Rusmir Mahmutcehajic, we have told them that if they try this, they will also drive out Croats." [Interpretation] Mr. Ambassador, did you report those who had delegated you about these drastic findings?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were not findings. These were assertions by the Bosnian Croats. They were not accurate. I've already reported to the Chamber that in many aspects the Bosnian Croat position and the Bosnian Serb position was congruent, was parallel, sometimes even identical. This is one of those positions where both the Bosnian Croats and the Bosnian Serbs were claiming that the Muslims wanted to eliminate them. It should be noted that at this time, January 12th, 1993, the Bosnian Croat Army was engaged in the heaviest ethnic cleansing in Central Bosnia. The Prlic case before the Tribunal, at which I have testified, is about that. So one has to judge these statements about the horrific things that were supposed to be done to the Croats, was not happening, where what was really happening was that the Croats were cleaning up the Muslims in Central Bosnia. Of course, I wrote down what Akmadzic said. I thought it was important. I underlined it, I put an asterisk next to it, and it indicated to me at the time, and I've not changed my view, that the Bosnian Serbs and Bosnian Croats indeed held identical positions to dismember Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ambassador. We will have to refute that, because, indeed, it is not correct, and we're going to prove that it is not correct. Do you know that Mile Akmadzic is a Croat, not a Serb, and that Mile Akmadzic was at the very source of information, as secretary-general of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, who had insight into everything that was going on? Is that not the case? Please, wherever possible, let's have a yes-or-no answer, because, indeed, we are wasting a lot of time with lengthy answers.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: And lengthy questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mile Akmadzic was the prime minister of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. We dealt with him frequently on a routine basis, so of course I knew who Mile Akmadzic was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you are not denying that from the elections in 1990, until the begin of the war, he was secretary-general of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ambassador, are you telling us that both Serb and Croat politicians presented a fundamental fear to you; namely, that the Muslim side, headed by Alija Izetbegovic, that is to say, this type of Muslims, not Abdic, Zulfikarpasic, and the others, but these Muslims, rather, have the intention to set up a unitary Islamic Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and that you did not believe either the Serbs or the Croats?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We believed that the Bosnian Muslim sought a unitary state. We did not believe and there's no evidence, no serious evidence, to prove that they wanted an Islamic Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina during the period of the war. All the statements you have cited come from one or two decades -- 10 or 20 years before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, do you know that the "Islamic Declaration" was republished in 1990 and that it was sold freely and distributed freely? Izetbegovic signed it as its author, so he thereby confirmed his authorship.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do we agree that he was tried for the materialisation of "The Islamic Declaration" in 1983, so that was only seven years before that, not 20 years before?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was tried in 1983, and the documents you cited, some of them were from the early 1970s.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But the reprint was there in 1990, thereby confirming his authorship. You also confirm that you remember that in order to have an easing of tensions in the political situation in the autumn of 1991, I asked Izetbegovic to renounce "The Islamic Declaration," to state publicly that that would not be his state and political programme, and you recalled that he did not actually do that; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the autumn of 1991, that happened, and you also walked out very ostentatiously on October 14th, 1991, from the Bosnian Assembly. And you said, I'm sure you remember, that if Bosnia declared itself independent, that would lead the parties to hell, particularly the Bosnian Muslims. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That's not the way it was, but we'll get to that. Mr. Ambassador, you said a few moments ago that if the quality of the state of Belgium were to be changed against the will of one of the communities, that would not be legitimate. What about the Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina? Why did they not enjoy the same right, to be asked about drastic changes in the state status of Bosnia-Herzegovina? The question of the Assembly on the 14th of October, 1991, is precisely that. Why are you denying the Serbs the right to have a decisive say of that kind if there is a drastic change in the federal -- in one of the federal units of the SFRY?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody denied the Bosnian Serbs the opportunity to speak. Indeed, it was a self-denial because a referendum was held - we've discussed this already - on February 29 and March 1, 1992, on the question of independence, and the Bosnian Serb party chose not to participate in that referendum. So it was a self-denial, Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You will see that that was not the case and that on the 24th and on the 25th of January, we proposed the following and agreed with Muhamed Cengic, not Hasan Cengic, and we did this in public, in the Assembly, that the government carry out a regionalisation and that then the Serbs would take part in the referendum. Regardless of how they would vote, they would vote in the referendum. You raised quite a few issues here, but now I would like to take you back to document 1D167. It has to do with the well-known "Islamic Declaration," which from its very inception in 1970 to the present day remained the basis for the future Bosnia-Herzegovina under the domination of the SDA, or, rather, the Muslims. Page 30, 29 in e-court. The English version is 29 in e-court. Yes, on the first page you saw that it was authored by Alija Izetbegovic, and we are looking at the reprint of 1990. And now page 29 in e-court, on the document itself, on this page: [In English] "First and foremost on these conclusions is certainly the incompatibility of Islam with non-Islamic systems. There can be neither peace nor co-existence between the Islamic religion and non-Islamic social and political instructions. The failure of --" [Interpretation] I can't see the rest. All right. Do you see this, Mr. Ambassador? This was published at the point in time when we were establishing the first democratic government, a coalition government, in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you disbelieve this? If you did not believe the Serbs and Croats, do you disbelieve Izetbegovic as well when he writes this?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that he wrote this earlier and signed it later. I also believe it had no practical effect within the SDA, neither then nor to this present day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now like to call up page 46 in e-court, the same document. While we're waiting for that to appear: I now have to envy Mr. Izetbegovic. What an advocate he has in you. So even in the other world, he must be feeling good.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I doubt that. As you know, the Bosnian Muslims refused to sign the Vance-Owen Peace Plan, along with you. It -- that was in January 1993. It took several months, until March 25, 1993, before Izetbegovic signed the peace plan, and then he only did so after the map had been changed to ensure Bosnian Serb rejection, because the corridor was cut by a Muslim province. So that I don't think it's fair to say that Izetbegovic, whether he's looking down on us or up at us, thinks he has an advocate in me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like to call up -- oh, actually, we have the page. Now, let us have a look at this: [In English] "... a rebirth, we are not announcing an age of peace and security, but one of unrest and trial. There are too many things crying out to be destroyed. There will not be days of prosperity, but of self-respect. A people which is asleep can be awakened only by blows. Whoever wishes our community well will not try to spare its struggle, danger and misfortune." [Interpretation] This position of Mr. Izetbegovic, does it not state that rebirth does not announce peace and security, but rather unrest and trial, and that whoever wishes well to the Islamic community should not spare it of suffering, danger, and misfortune? Were you aware of that position?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the whole, yes. I was not aware specifically of "Women and the Family," Chapter 14, but we knew that Izetbegovic was on the -- was on the religious side of the SDA.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the Prlic case which you referred to, yourself, on the 4th of February, 2007, on transcript page 16866, you said: [In English] "It's incorrect to say that Izetbegovic wasn't concerned about the well-being of others." [Interpretation] It is other peoples or ethnic communities that are referred to. And I'm telling you, Mr. Ambassador, that Izetbegovic did not care about the well-being of the Muslim people, let alone the well-being of the Serb and Croat people. What do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I say that's a debatable point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like to call up page 55 in e-court of the document, itself. In e-court, it's 55, but it says "46." Let us see where this is. In the middle, in the middle, and it says: [In English] " ... should not -- should again start to take over power as soon as it is morally and numerically strong enough to be able to overturn not only the existing non-Islamic government, but also to build up a new Islamic one. This differentiation is important ..." [Interpretation] Are you denying that these are instructions for a political coup by non-democratic means, not when they have a Muslim state, in terms of percentage, but when they simply feel strong enough to carry this through?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we can parse the language in different ways, but it says "numerically strong enough," so I'm sure that means at the ballot box. In any case, as we agree, taken together the Bosnian Serb population of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Bosnian Croat population outnumbered the Bosnian Muslim population, so their having a numeric majority against both the Bosnian Croats and the Bosnian Serbs was impossible. And since you and Dr. -- you and Mate Boban had good relations - recall the meetings in Graz in May 1992, after the fighting started, you and Mate met in Austria - so I think the chances of the Muslims against your group and Mate Boban's Croats really was nil.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, do you have more questions about this "Islamic Declaration"?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you're not denying the fact that if they had a chance to do this, that they would do it against us?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's precisely what I am denying, Dr. Karadzic. You're reading into what is a manifesto, with very little chance of being realised in reality, you're reading a whole series of actions into it. I don't think that's justified.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We'll show after the break that things developed exactly as stated in "The Islamic Declaration." Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Unless it is objected to, this "Islam Declaration --"

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- will be admitted --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D75.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- as Exhibit D75. Thank you. We'll have a half-hour break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just have one scheduling inquiry to make. I can do that now or do that at the end of the session, but I just wanted to have an opportunity to raise a query with the Court about scheduling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We will hear from you at the end of this session. Mr. Karadzic, please go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, you knew quite a bit about the activities of the UNHCR, particularly with respect to supplies, supplying the population with humanitarian food stuffs and medical items; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Ambassador, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it true that all three ethnic communities depended, to a great extent, on the aid and assistance given by the UNHCR?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's true in varying degrees, and it would take too much time to go into which geographic sections were better supplied than the other. But as a general proposition, that is accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, let me help you out. Perhaps it was only Herceg-Bosna that was in a slightly better position, because Croatia wasn't under sanctions, and Serbia was, and Republika Srpska was also under sanctions from Serbia. But it is a fact that all three communities, especially the Muslims and Serbs, needed the UNHCR assistance and the assistance of the Red Cross; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, we saw earlier on, when we were looking at the judgement to Alija Izetbegovic and his group, which in the 1990s won the elections, and on pages 140 and 141 of the Serbian version, we saw that the judge, whose name was Hodzic -- or, rather, the chamber concluded that the realisation of Izetbegovic's goals was only possible in three ways: With a fratricidal war, terror, or a foreign intervention. I'd like now -- well, my case is, and I'm going to prove and show that here, that Mr. Izetbegovic wasn't satisfied with just a fratricidal war and terror, but needed foreign intervention, and this judge saw this, but he was modest and mentioned each of these three components as being able to bring about those goals. He was sort of clairvoyant. And now he had this third point, foreign intervention. Now, the SDA leadership, was it very persistent in asking for and expecting international military intervention? Just yes or no, please, and then we can move on.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. I'd now like to draw your attention to your notebook, notebook number 5, which is Prosecution 65 ter 06538, page 35, dealing with your meeting with General Morillon on the 12th of December, 1992. So I'd like to have that document called up, please, notebook number 5, Prosecution 65 ter 06538 document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, in the future when you cite the exhibit, please use the exhibit number instead of 65 ter number. This is Exhibit P788.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellency. Well, we prepared it this way because of the Ambassador's statements, and we found the need, in the course of these proceedings, during the trial, to introduce new elements.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, here General Morillon -- well, this is what you recorded: [In English] "Mr. Izetbegovic and the radical wing of the Presidency wants to provoke foreign intervention." [Interpretation] And then Morillon: [In English] "Foreign intervention. The B and H government was very unhappy when the UNHCR convoy got through to the Muslim town of Srebrenica." [Interpretation] So I now put it to you that we have sufficient proof and evidence to show that the SDA abused the sufferings of its people in order to bring about the sympathies of the international community and thereby a military intervention against the Serbs. Do you exclude that or deny it?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is the case that the Bosnian government desired foreign intervention, since, as we mentioned earlier, they were losing the war, they were being ethnically cleansed, Sarajevo was being shelled on a daily basis since April 1992. Indeed, it was shelled for three solid years. But you asked earlier whether they expected foreign intervention; not just that they hoped for it, did they expect it. And the answer to that is, no, they did not did not expect it because they were realistic and they could see that neither the United States, nor the European Community, was about ready to do that. Now, you ask about good faith, did they want to attract the sympathy of the world. And they did. And, in fact, it was easy -- you made it easy for them, particularly by the shelling of Sarajevo. You may recall that Lord Owen said that to you directly on more than one occasion. He asked you why did you continue shelling Sarajevo when it was giving you such a bad public press, and you never answered him. But they -- yes, they all -- all the parties took advantage, to the degree possible, of UNHCR food deliveries.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, now with respect to Sarajevo and everything else, we're going to show what the real truth was here, but let's focus on this now: Did the Muslim side abuse the sufferings of its people, of its own people, in order to win over -- in order to -- well, did they persistently ask for foreign intervention and didn't they abuse the sufferings of their own people to win over the sympathies of the international community and bring about a foreign intervention, in view of what General Morillon informed you of?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not say they abused it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But General Morillon says here that the Muslim government was unhappy because the convoy had, indeed, reached Srebrenica. How do you explain that and interpret that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have to go to the previous page, Dr. Karadzic, where he says: "Izetbegovic and the radical wing of the Presidency want to provoke foreign intervention." As we have discussed here today on numerous occasions, a point I've made to you frequently, and I don't think you disagree with it, was that the SDA was not united. It had wings of the party. So he's talking about one group, but he's not saying that this was the position of everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ambassador. But General Morillon here is not referring to the SDA, but the Bosnian government. And on that same page, you can see and you recorded that: "Ganic yesterday told Morillon that --" [In English] "Confidence conditions needed to be imposed by force." [Interpretation] So there was no doubt that everybody was united. But let's stay with this. General Morillon did inform you that the government was unhappy because the humanitarian aid had reached Srebrenica; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's in my note, so the answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could explain to us in what context he said so, Ambassador.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the government was difficult in that respect. They sought -- they were desperate. This was early December. They'd been at war since March. They were losing all the way through, and losing on every front, so they tried to gain sympathy as much as they could. And Morillon, a very capable and good man, understood this. But it would be inaccurate to draw the conclusion that somehow they had started the whole thing or they were expecting to profit from it, because the mere fact that they were losing so decisively clearly shows that they were not prepared for this war. I mean, after all, the Yugoslav Army, the JNA, an army of several hundred thousand well-armed people, had, already in May of 1992, taken the non-Bosnian soldiers away, but left their equipment, most of their men, their machinery, and the army then declared itself the Army of the Republika Srpska, the VRS, so that there was just no comparison between the sides, militarily. And by this time, December 1992, more than a million people had been displaced and ethnically cleansed, most of them Muslims. Again, President Sommaruga of the ICRC, in August of 1992, used the figure several hundred thousand, and this was already three months later, during the heaviest period, so that it is not a surprise to see that this desperate party tried to take desperate measures. On the other hand, it should be pointed out that the convoys got through, Srebrenica was resupplied, Bratunac was resupplied. People expected that the winter of 1992/1993 would see one million deaths -- one million deaths in Bosnia and Herzegovina. That was widely predicted by the press and by governments. And UNPROFOR and UNHCR, and the ICRC to a lesser degree, above all UNPROFOR, which was given the mandate of protecting the humanitarian supplies - that was the mandate, it was not a fighting force - they did a superb job and nobody died in the winter of 1992/1993, not on the Bosnian Muslim side, not on the Bosnian Croat side, not on the Bosnian Serb side. I think that has to be taken into account.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ambassador. Please go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, and where did the other armies come from, where were they created -- what were they created from? Where did General Delic come from, for instance? What about the JNA reservists; did they make up the Patriotic League, and so on? Do you want to say that the JNA only belonged to the Serbs, came to belong to the Serbs in Bosnia, or was the JNA a basis for all the armies in the former Yugoslavia? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to say that the JNA was the basis for all the armies is completely inaccurate. The overwhelming force of the JNA supported the Bosnian Serbs because, after all, even after it stopped being the Yugoslav People's Army and became the JA, the Yugoslav Army, it was essentially the Serb army. After all, Croatia and Slovenia and Macedonia -- I mean, everybody else was out of the republic, so it was the Serb army, and it was the best equipped. Not only that, with respect to Dr. Karadzic's army, namely, the VRS, the Army of the Republika Srpska, it received supplies. There was no surprise about that. We could observe it. The UNPROFOR could see the supplies coming across the Drina, that is, military supplies. And the salaries of the troops in the Republika Srpska Army were paid from Belgrade. So, Dr. Karadzic, when you say everybody participated in the JNA, I mean, that's really not accurate. Your side got 98 per cent of the JNA help.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ambassador. But none of what you said is true or correct. It's not true that the salaries for the army came from Serbia -- for the troops came from Serbia, but a number of officers who would otherwise have their salaries had they sat around cafes in Belgrade, that money -- and it was about 2.000 officers, it was that money. It's not that Serbia paid for the Army of Republika Srpska. It was officers who inherited from Yugoslavia that received the money, whether they were in Belgrade or elsewhere. But let's leave that to one side. The topic is this and the answer is this: Did the Muslim government abuse the sufferings of its population in order to provoke foreign intervention? And let me take you back to "The Islamic Declaration" and the judgement of 1983, which is Defence Exhibit 1D34, page 17 of the Serbian, where it says that the Muslims must be ready to sacrifice themselves in order to achieve their goals, self-sacrifice in order to achieve their goals. We don't have to go back to that, but do you remember it? It was up on our screens, that page. Or, for example -- yes, thank you. Or 1D167, page 146, where he says: [In English] "Prosperity which is asleep can be awakened only by blows. Whoever wishes our community well will not try to spare its struggle, danger, and misfortune." [Interpretation] Do you see ideological consequences in the behaviour and conduct of the Muslim government towards their own people, that they were -- they weren't arbitrary, but they were deeply founded on a belief, on a philosophy, political philosophy, that the people should suffer a great deal in order to return to Islam; yes or no? I accept any answer, yes, or no, or any other answer.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're saying, Dr. Karadzic -- you're implying and you're saying that: A, the Muslim people were suffering; B, they were suffering because the Muslim government wanted them to suffer. Now, that's not true. The reason they were suffering, the reason they were in detention centres and concentration camps, is that the Bosnian Serbs kicked them out of their houses, used force, intimidation, and violence, up to and including death, to expel them, and -- [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Shall we stop there? I'm going to challenge that.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you're doing is comparing the words of a decade earlier, that were re-signed in 1990, with the reality on the ground, and I think that's really not fair.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, your question warranted a long answer. Otherwise, you can give evidence on your own later on. So let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What I'm interested in now is this, and you say yes or no: Now, whether the Serbs expelled the Muslims from their homes, that's a subject that we'll come back to. We won't leave that uncovered and not dealt with. But let's stick to what we're discussing here and now. Do you know that I am being accused of exercising terror over the citizens of Sarajevo? I'd now like us to throw more light on the situation in Sarajevo to see what was actually going on there. Do you -- did you happen to follow my opening statement in this courtroom on the 1st and 2nd of March, or do you know about the substance of my opening statement here in court?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I neither followed it nor do I know the substance of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, as to my opening statement, did you discuss that with the Prosecutor when you attended your proofing session for your testimony here?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure that the proofing session shouldn't remain confidential. But, in fact, the answer is, no, I never discussed it with the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On the 11th of April of this year, did you give the Prosecutor some of the additional information which had not previously been contained in your statements and testimony?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I have document 1D287 next, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a document which we were given by the Prosecutor, and it contains additional information that you gave to them; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was an expansion of the discussion concerning the actions. It was not new in that sense. I regard this as an expansion of previous information. And the information is accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That means that you received information that Izetbegovic's government forces opened fire from the grounds of the main hospital in Sarajevo in order to provoke return fire from the Army of Republika Srpska; is that it?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's accurate as so stated in the document dated 11 April.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm interested here in the word "occasional." What did you mean was only occasional, how many times; monthly, yearly, or however?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was very rare. Our information, of course, came from the UNPROFOR troops who were stationed in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And that is according to UNPROFOR and what it established. How do you know it wasn't more frequent, or how do you know the major incidents weren't carried out by the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's two questions. As to the first question you asked, the reason we know it wasn't more frequent is that the UNPROFOR soldiers in Sarajevo were numerous. They weren't three or four people, there were hundreds of them, and they had very accurate observation points all around the city. Particularly, they had to do that to correctly assess the damage that was done by the Bosnian Serb shelling of the city. So they had good knowledge of what was going on all over the city. That's the answer to your first question. And as to your second question, they checked out very carefully the charges which were made at the time by the Bosnian Serb side, and specifically occasionally by Dr. Karadzic himself, that the Bosnian Serbs -- excuse me, that the Bosnian Muslims were firing on their own people. The Bosnian Serbs also maintained that occasionally the Bosnian Muslim soldiers dressed up in Bosnian Serb uniforms, or JNA uniforms, in order to fool the rest of the world into thinking that the Bosnian Serbs were attacking them. None of this fooled UNPROFOR, and they were very careful to give us their considered judgement; namely, that the Bosnian Serb shelling -- and they even gave us a shelling count. Every day, we received a number of the Bosnian Serb shells that landed in Sarajevo, so they were really very careful in their observation. And I think we were correct in believing them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When did you receive this information from them about the provocations by the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you made that accusation steadily through the negotiation, Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But I'm asking you, Mr. Ambassador, about this piece of information, this expansion of your statement that you gave on the 11th of April. When did you receive it from the observers?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall exactly when it was. I'm sorry, I just simply don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Certainly, during the time that you were there; right?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure of that. I may have learned of it when I saw the Secretary-General's letter to Izetbegovic. That's possible. I just can't be certain of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But during the war, that's certain; right?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, during the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: May I ask you why you didn't mention that in any of your statements or during any of your testimonies so far?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've tried to answer all your questions. I've said -- perhaps you've forgotten, but I've said that with regard to the mistreatment of people, whether it was ethnic cleansing or just general abuse, that it was reported to us by the International Committee of the Red Cross and by UNHCR that all three parties to the conflict abused prisoners, that the quality of the treatment was pretty much the same, but that the quantity, the amount of abuse, the amount of torture, the amount of coercion and expulsion, was overwhelmingly Bosnian Serb. I've already reported that and so stated during my testimony. In addition to that, Dr. Karadzic, you've had the benefit, as you should have, of my journals, which are over 2.000 pages in length, and I'm pleased to see that you read them carefully and that you understand that they are honestly meant and objective and neutral; criticising Izetbegovic, for example. So I've not in any case held anything back from this Tribunal. That I recall something after 18 years I don't think is surprising. Many people forgot things after 18 years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, can I go back to one thing, while I'm thinking about it. In your journal, you talk about the BiH government being upset that a humanitarian convoy got through to Srebrenica, and that's been a aligned to provoking international intervention, in the sense that if the convoys weren't getting through, it would be more likely that there would be foreign intervention. First and foremost, is that the connection?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that's the direction in which the question wanted to take the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Right. And, secondly, you were there at the time. What's your assessment of the realpolitik? Would a failure of humanitarian aid getting through at that time have provoked foreign intervention or was there reluctance to intervene overwhelming.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The reluctance to intervene was overwhelming.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'm just waiting for the interpretation to finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, did you find out or hear from UNPROFOR, or from the Western media, or from UN reports that had not been made public, that the Muslim forces in Sarajevo killed their very own citizens and presented them as victims of Serb shelling; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were aware of your statements to that effect. We never received information of that nature from UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you preclude that possibility? Do you rule out the possibility of such UNPROFOR reports and reports coming from other foreign observers and authorities? Do you rule that possibility out, that that's the way it was? It can be either three "no"s or three "yes"s.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you say the Muslim forces killed their very own citizens. I would -- I'm not asking you, but in order to answer that I'd have to know what you mean by that. For example, you could say they put their own citizens in the line of fire, or they sauved their own citizens. I'm not certain what that question means. I don't think it's true, but I don't want to be definitive when the question, itself, was so indefinite.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The question was whether you knew about it, either from officials or from the Western media, but you have given your answer. Thank you. Can we now look at document 1D486. While we're waiting for it, I will give a brief explanation. It has to do with a report of the Security Administration of the Supreme Command of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Now let us see whether there is an English version. If not, I'm just going to read out a small portion of it. In Serbian, we can move on to the next page ending with numbers 228. This is what it says, the report of the Muslim Intelligence Service: "The Military Security Service reached new information to the effect that citizens of Serb ethnicity at Dobrinja are being treated as second-rate citizens and that pressure is being exerted against them so that they would move out of that locality. In effect, a reliable source stated that there are cases of physical mistreatment, unlawful arrests, and even denial of humanitarian aid to persons of Serb ethnicity, which causes revolt and fear among the citizens." He mentioned the example of a person who has not been receiving humanitarian aid for a few months already only on account of the fact that the person is a Serb. The son of that person was physically mistreated several times by armed individuals, without any cause, so he sustained grievous bodily injury: "What is indicative is the killing at Dobrinja a few months ago of a certain individual by the name of Mercep, although the authorities presented it as death as a result of shelling. Actually, the guilt of the killed Mercep was allegedly because he did not return to Dobrinja on time, after he was allowed to go to town in order to take his wife into hospital."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could we please have the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "On the other hand, threat were made to the effect that they shouldn't tell anyone about it."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you trust the military security of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In what respect are you asking the question? I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, the person is registered as being a victim of the shelling, whereas he was killed because he just arrived late.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you quoted from a document that says that, and I have read the document. That's all I know about it. That does not really have any bearing on the three-years-long shelling of Sarajevo by the Bosnian Serb forces under General Mladic's command. We've already said and established, and I assume you agree, that all three sides committed abuses. That's in the record. So finding this or that case, unfortunately, is not very difficult because it was an ugly war, and there are other indicators of who received most of the abuse. The fact that there were over a million Muslim -- [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- refuges expelled from Bosnia by your troops gives us an indication of the numbers involved, and I think, Dr. Karadzic, we really do have to bear that in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ambassador. However, that is not correct. You mentioned December 1992. That is exactly when it was published in the "Jerusalem Post" that there are more Serb refugees than Croat and Muslim refugees put together. Are you denying that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's false. That is totally false and demonstrably false. We have the account from the ICRC. They took the refugees out. The "Jerusalem Post" is an English-language newspaper published in Israel. It can barely cover Israeli events, much less events in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ambassador, I'm afraid we won't have time to deal with everything, and that I will have to ask for additional time. You have opened different issues, and you are resorting to tu quoque. As for ethnic cleansing, we are going to do a separate cross-examination. 1D337 is the document I'd like to deal with now. This is also a document from the Security Administration of the Main Staff of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I would like to ask you not to confuse issues. The topic we're dealing now is what the Muslims are doing to their very own people, with the intention of leading to an international intervention by blackening the name of the Serbs. You said that you do not believe that. Now I'm giving you proof of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, are you minded to tender the Ambassador's supplemental information sheet, which is actually a proofing note?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Excellency; not only that, but also the document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll come to that. If there is no objection, that will be admitted as what number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D76, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Tieger, how about the BiH document about the killing of civilians allegedly by a shell, yes, 486?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Two quick issues, Your Honour. Number one, it wasn't translated, so we would certainly need an opportunity to review it. Number two, I have no objection to that, in principle. I would also note, however, that that is not one that directly each merges from this witness, but is a submission by Dr. Karadzic in support of his point. But mainly the issue is that we received no translation whatsoever, so we do need to look it over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll mark it for identification, pending translation, with what number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D77, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellencies, in relation to what was stated just now, I would like to say that it is the Prosecutor who made all this possible for me, or, rather, led me to do this, because he raised a great many issues with this witness. And the witness, himself, made assertions that go beyond the scope of the direct examination, so I simply have to deal with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, do you believe or do you rule out the possibility of the following: when I say that the Muslim Army killed foreign soldiers, UN soldiers, with a view to tarnishing the image of the Serb side?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, we knew at the time that it was most probable that the French peacekeepers had been killed by Muslim fire. It's in my journals, and that was something that was widely understood by the UN troops. It was never proved, but it was assumed to be the case. We also knew that Bosnian Muslim elements, mainly criminal elements, in Sarajevo had killed some soldiers of the JNA at the very beginning of the war, when they were withdrawing from Sarajevo. I'm sure Dr. Karadzic will recall that. So I think it's fair to say we were pretty well informed or perhaps quite well informed about the goings on inside Sarajevo. One could not say that we knew everything. I don't think that's ever possible. But the troops did a very good job of keeping us and their headquarters informed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. In relation to the beginning of the war, yes, that's the way it was, but I have a document here that pertains to the 26th and 27th of October, 1993; that is to say, a year and a half into the war. And this practice continued nevertheless. Allow me to read that. We actually have a translation of it, that particular section: "The UNPROFOR Command for Sector Sarajevo has information that the shells that fell on the 20th of October, 1993, in Sector Bravo (our unit positions)," that is to say, the Muslim positions, "at elevation 930613, in the north-east part of Sarajevo, came from the Bravo position," also our positions, "at elevation 9162. They informed the UNPROFOR Command in Kiseljak of this. According to information from the SDB, the French Battalion Command is investigating the sniper wounding of one of their soldiers from the FraBat II squadron stationed in the eastern part of Skenderija. In connection to this, Colonel Duburg said that most likely the shot came from close range and assessed that this effectively rules out the Serb from Grbavica. He said that due to this, further investigations will concentrate on the 10th Brigade of the Army of the Republic of BH, whose soldiers they believe most likely to have caused this incident." Do you see that that happened not only in the beginning of the war, but also in October of 1993?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, you said that it had never been proven. In that case, I would like to see your journal number 2. 06535 is the Prosecution number. I don't know what the exhibit number is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You can give the 65 ter number, five digits.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 06535, page 67.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Exhibit P785.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Page 67, on the right-hand side of the screen. Now, Morillon, parentheses: [In English] " ...will discuss this tomorrow with Karadzic and Ganic, wants Ganic to admit that Sandzak killed the two French UNPROFOR soldiers. In break, Ganic has already admitted this privately." [Interpretation] So it was established after all, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I said, I reported it in my notes, and you've just confirmed what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, but earlier on you said that that had never been proven, but you suspected that, rightly so. And now it seems that it was stated so by the perpetrators, admitted by the perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, earlier on you didn't mention which specific case you were talking about. You simply said "French soldiers." If you had been specific, we would have known that. And I was answering your general question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That was my question about the phenomenon, itself, not each and every individual case. I asked whether they did that kind of thing, and now we see they did. Thank you. Let's move on. Now I'd like us to look at your journal number 1, Prosecution 06534, on page 33, your meeting with Generals Nambiar and Morillon on the 9th of September, 1992. Do we have it? Now, this is what Mr. Nambiar says at that meeting with you, on the right-hand side. I don't know whether Mr. Vance was there as well, but you certainly wrote this down." Nambiar in relation to Sarajevo: [In English] "Since third week of August, UNPROFOR is being deliberately targeted by Muslim troops, have protested this to Izetbegovic."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [In English] "Nambiar: Incidents of killing of two French soldiers yesterday was bastardly [sic] act cold-blooded ambush by Muslim force of Presidency. The humanitarian convoy announced in advance, as always, unquestionably 100 per cent certain that French soldiers were killed by Muslim forces." [Interpretation] Do you remember that meeting? And is a greater authority needed than General Nambiar to say that 100 per cent?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I remember the meeting. Incidentally, the word is dastardly, not bastardly. Excuse me. And you'll notice that the next dash says: "Probable, but not certain, that Italian plane was shot down by Croat forces." An Italian plane had been shot down in that period of September 1992. I mentioned this to indicate what I have said before consistently, that all three sides committed abuses and committed heinous acts, to be sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, please, do you know what the consequences was of the downing of that Italian plane? Did that lead to a ban on Serb flights?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There had been discussion since the beginning of the war about air activity over Bosnia and Herzegovina. The only force that had an air force was the Bosnian Serbs. Croatians occasionally over-flew Bosnia, but that was very rare. The Muslims had essentially nothing in the air, due to their weakness. So the question arose - Dr. Karadzic is correct - about Serbian air activity over Bosnia and Herzegovina, for the reason I've just mentioned. And to continue, I'm sure this is what he's going to -- where he's going, and it's important to know, that after some time the United Nations Security Council passed a resolution on a no-fly zone, making Bosnia-Herzegovina a no-fly zone, primarily to deter the Bosnian Serb Air Force. And we had many conversations, Dr. Karadzic, and the negotiators and me, on this subject. You'll find them all recorded in my diaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you. My question was whether the downing of this plane, and the first allegations in this respect were that this had been done by the Serbs, was that something that triggered the ban on flights, the introduction of the no-fly zone? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll prove that later. Mr. Ambassador, as for all of this that was in your journals, why did you not state that at any one of your testimonies up until now? Don't you think that that would have worked in the favour of the accused, Krajisnik, Prlic, and others, had you testified to the effect that there was this phenomenon of committing evil in order to blacken the other side? An impartial witness would rightly be expected to do that; right?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I did do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In which case?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This case, on numerous occasions. You haven't perhaps been listening carefully enough. And in the Prlic case, I was asked, for example, by the defendants, who were Croats, Were we the only people who committed ethnic cleansing in Central Bosnia in 1993, and my answer to that was, No. In earlier cases, I gave the same answers. I come back, Dr. Karadzic, to what I've said several times, but which you are understandably ignoring; namely, that we were told and understood that all three parties committed crimes of abuse, of ethnic cleansing, and that the overwhelming number of those crimes were on the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to prove that that is not the case. But now we are dealing with the commission of evil in order to blacken the other side. The highest military authority, UNPROFOR, confirmed with 100 per cent certainty that that was done by the Muslims. Did you say that in any one of the cases where you testified, Krajisnik or Prlic, would that have worked in their favour or against them, in those cases? Had you come out saying that, that the Muslim side did that with such intentions ?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two points. I always said it when I was asked about it. Second point: We were receiving reports, for example, that the shell count on Sarajevo per day from the Serb gunners in the hills was 3.000 to 5.000, three -- [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, let me finish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 3.000 to 5.000, I mention, because it shows that it's possible, that when one counts 3.000 to 5.000, that one might miss a shell here or two or even be inaccurate about it, because the shelling of Sarajevo was that heavy. So I don't think we should blame UNPROFOR if they sometimes missed something or sometimes got something wrong, because they got -- the main point was very clear. You may recall that I kept in my office in Geneva, at the conference, a graph on the wall, a daily graph of the shell count of your troops on Sarajevo and of the Bosnian Muslim return fire, which was, on average, about 300 shots from weapons of lower calibre. So 3.000 against 300 gives you an idea of the intensity and who was doing what to whom. I'm sorry, Dr. Karadzic, but I must point this out to the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But, Mr. Ambassador, when asked the question of whether the Muslims obstructed the delivery of humanitarian aid, you have this piece of information where Mr. Nambiar says humanitarian convoys were targeted, and now I'm sticking to one topic, staying with one topic; that the Muslims, in conformity with "The Islamic Declaration," tried to harm their people, in the humanitarian respect, and that they were ready to kill foreign soldiers for that purpose, and that they wanted to blame the Serbs for the killings and for the lack of supplies. And it says so loud and clear in your notebook, and I ask why you didn't say that during the other trials.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure that I didn't say it. Perhaps I was never asked on that point. But it is clear, and this was known at the time, that the Bosnian Muslim government was desperate for foreign intervention. They said so publicly, and that was no secret since they were losing so badly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. I think that's it for today, Ambassador Okun. We'll start again tomorrow morning, but before that I will -- Ambassador, you are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Do you have any objection to this document, 337?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, it's the same situation as the previous document, Your Honour, with respect to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think we have a translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just a very partial translation. I think the Prosecution should have an opportunity to review the remainder of the document to see if any portions are applicable in context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let me check.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We don't oppose that, but we're just offering this portion because that's the relevant part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't see the need to translate the other part. Do you have objection to admit only this part which was translated?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, I don't have any objection, in principle, to the tendering or admission of that portion. I do think it's fair for the Prosecution to have an opportunity to see if any other aspects of the document -- I'm not suggesting getting it translated in toto, but that we should have an opportunity to review it to see if other portions bear on the tendered portion and illuminate that in context. That's my only issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My question was: Unless it is admitted into evidence, you don't have access to the document, itself?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, if the Court -- if we -- I have no objection to it being admitted. Should we find that there are other portions that are relevant and we tender it then, that's a fine way to proceed as well. I have no problem with that approach. I'm only indicating that when there's a partial translation of a document, and we have not yet had an opportunity to see if other portions may bear on that submitted portion, that at some point we should have the opportunity to bring to the Court's attention other aspects of the same document that perhaps should be tendered as well in connection with the one excerpt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Okay. I see that that will be admitted as it is now. And then which is the number for it?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit D78.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Tieger, very briefly?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The next scheduled witness, Your Honour, is due to travel tomorrow. As the Court is aware, given the current schedule, if she were not able to begin her testimony, which seems likely, much less complete it, which I think seems even more unlikely, she would have to return home and then come back again. Given the pace of proceedings and the amount of material that appears remains to be covered, and the number of requested hours, I would suggest it may be more fair to that particular witness not to ask her to arrive tomorrow and wait, but to bring her after this week, the following week. But I didn't want to take that step without consulting with the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think that's a more plausible step. But, Dr. Karadzic, how much longer do you have for this witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Excellency, at least as much as I had asked for. And please believe me, I'll probably need more time, because I'm not sure that the witness is not using too much of my time up. And we can see that through the satisfaction expressed by Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, with that observation, it seems not practical that we start the next witness this week. Tomorrow, 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 27th day of April, 2010, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.46 p.m.,
